mn138:1.2: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
mn138:1.3: There the Buddha addressed the bhikkhus,
mn138:2.1: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you a summary recital and its analysis.
mn138:2.2: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”
mn138:3.1: “A bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that, as he examines, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally, nor stuck internally; and by not clinging, he would not be agitated.
mn138:3.2: When this is the case, there is no coming to be of the origin of suffering—of rebirth, old age, and death in the future.”
mn138:4.1: That is what the Buddha said.
mn138:4.2: When he had spoken, the Holy One got up from his seat and entered his dwelling.
mn138:5.1: Soon after the Buddha left, those bhikkhus considered,
mn138:5.2: “The Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail.
mn138:5.5: Who can explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha?”
mn138:5.7: “This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.
mn138:5.8: He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.
mn138:5.9: Let’s go to him, and ask him about this matter.”
mn138:6.1: Then those bhikkhus went to Mahākaccāna, and exchanged greetings with him.
mn138:6.2: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. They told him what had happened, and said,
mn138:7.1: “Reverends, suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But he’d pass over the roots and trunk, imagining that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves.
mn138:7.2: Such is the consequence for the venerables. Though you were face to face with the Buddha, you bypassed him, imagining that you should ask me about this matter.
mn138:7.3: For he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the teacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.
mn138:7.4: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.
mn138:7.5: You should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”
mn138:8.1: “Certainly he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the teacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.
mn138:8.2: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.
mn138:8.3: We should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.
mn138:8.4: Still, Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.
mn138:8.5: He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.
mn138:8.6: Please explain this, if it’s no trouble.”
mn138:9.1: “Well then, reverends, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”
mn138:9.4: “Reverends, the Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail:
mn138:9.5: ‘A bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated. If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.’
mn138:9.6: This is how I understand the detailed meaning of this summary recital.
mn138:10.1: How is consciousness said to be scattered and diffused externally?
mn138:10.2: In this case, when a bhikkhu sees a sight with their eyes, and consciousness follows after the features of that sight—tied, attached, and fettered to the attraction in its features—consciousness is said to be scattered and diffused externally.
mn138:10.3: When they hear a sound with their ears …
mn138:10.4: When they smell an odor with their nose …
mn138:10.5: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …
mn138:10.6: When they feel a touch with their body …
mn138:10.7: When they know an idea with their mind, and consciousness follows after the features of that idea—tied, attached, and fettered to the attraction in its features—consciousness is said to be scattered and diffused externally.
mn138:10.8: That’s how consciousness is said to be scattered and diffused externally.
mn138:11.1: And how is consciousness said to be not scattered and diffused externally?
mn138:11.2: In this case, when a bhikkhu sees a sight with their eyes, but consciousness does not follow after the features of that sight—not tied, attached, and fettered to the attraction in its features—consciousness is said to be not scattered and diffused externally.
mn138:11.3: When they hear a sound with their ears …
mn138:11.4: When they smell an odor with their nose …
mn138:11.5: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …
mn138:11.6: When they feel a touch with their body …
mn138:11.7: When they know an idea with their mind, but consciousness does not follow after the features of that idea—not tied, attached, and fettered to the attraction in its features—consciousness is said to be not scattered and diffused externally.
mn138:11.8: That’s how consciousness is said to be not scattered and diffused externally.
mn138:12.1: And how is it said to be stuck internally?
mn138:12.2: Take a bhikkhu who, fully withdrawn from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and dwells in the first stage of meditation, which has the delight and contentment born of seclusion, with thinking and considering.
mn138:12.3: When consciousness follows after that delight and contentment born of seclusion—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that delight and contentment born of seclusion—the mind is said to be stuck internally.
mn138:13.1: Furthermore, as thinking and considering are stilled, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second stage of meditation, which has the delight and contentment born of concentration, with internal clarity and poise, without thinking and considering.
mn138:13.2: When consciousness follows after that delight and contentment born of concentration—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that delight and contentment born of concentration—the mind is said to be stuck internally.
mn138:14.1: Furthermore, with the fading away of delight, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the third stage of meditation, where they meditate with equanimity, with awareness and comprehension, personally experiencing the contentment of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and aware, one meditates content.’
mn138:14.2: When consciousness follows after that equanimity—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that bliss with equanimity—the mind is said to be stuck internally.
mn138:15.1: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth stage of meditation, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and awareness.
mn138:15.2: When consciousness follows after that neutral feeling—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that neutral feeling—the mind is said to be stuck internally.
mn138:15.3: That’s how it is said to be stuck internally.
mn138:16.1: And how is it said to be not stuck internally?
mn138:16.2: It’s when a bhikkhu, fully withdrawn from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and dwells in the first stage of meditation, which has the delight and contentment born of seclusion, with thinking and considering.
mn138:16.3: When consciousness does not follow after that delight and contentment born of seclusion—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that delight and contentment born of seclusion—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.
mn138:17.1: Furthermore, they enter the second stage of meditation …
mn138:17.2: When consciousness does not follow after that delight and contentment born of concentration—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that delight and contentment born of concentration—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.
mn138:18.1: Furthermore, they enter and dwell in the third stage of meditation …
mn138:18.2: When consciousness does not follow after that equanimity—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that bliss with equanimity—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.
mn138:19.1: Furthermore, they enter and dwell in the fourth stage of meditation …
mn138:19.2: When consciousness does not follow after that neutral feeling—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that neutral feeling—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.
mn138:19.3: That’s how it is said to be not stuck internally.
mn138:20.1: And how is it agitated because of grasping?
mn138:20.2: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.
mn138:20.3: He regards form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.
mn138:20.4: But that form changes and is unstable,
mn138:20.5: and his consciousness alters in accordance with the change in form.
mn138:20.6: With the agitation born from the alteration in accordance with the change in form and coming from the co-arising of (unskillful mental) qualities, his mind stays consumed.
mn138:20.7: And because of the consumption of awareness, he feels fearful, threatened, and solicitous...
mn138:20.8: He assumes feeling to be the self …
mn138:20.11: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
mn138:20.12: But that consciousness changes and is unstable,
mn138:20.13: and his consciousness alters in accordance with the change in consciousness.
mn138:20.14: With the agitation born from the alteration in accordance with the change in consciousness and coming from the co-arising of (unskillful mental) qualities, his mind stays consumed.
mn138:20.15: And because of the consumption of awareness, he feels fearful, threatened, and solicitous...
mn138:20.16: That’s how it is agitated because of grasping.
mn138:21.1: And how is it not agitated because of grasping?
mn138:21.2: It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.
mn138:21.3: He doesn’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.
mn138:21.4: His form changes and is unstable,
mn138:21.5: but his consciousness doesn’t—because of the change & instability of form—alter in accordance with the change in form.
mn138:21.6: His mind is not consumed with any agitation born from an alteration in accordance with the change in form or coming from the co-arising of (unskillful mental) qualities.
mn138:21.7: And because his awareness is not consumed, he feels neither fearful, threatened, nor solicitous.
mn138:21.8: He doesn’t assume feeling feeling to be the self …
mn138:21.11: consciousness as the self, the self as having consciousness, consciousness in the self, or the self in consciousness.
mn138:21.12: His consciousness changes and is unstable,
mn138:21.13: but it doesn’t doesn’t—because of the change & instability of consciousness—alter in accordance with the change in consciousness.
mn138:21.14: His mind is not consumed with any agitation born from an alteration in accordance with the change in consciousness or coming from the co-arising of (unskillful mental) qualities.
mn138:21.15: And because his awareness is not consumed, he feels neither fearful, threatened, nor solicitous.
mn138:21.16: That’s how it is not agitated because of clinging/sustenance.
mn138:22.1: The Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail:
mn138:22.2: ‘A bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that, as he examines, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally, nor stuck internally; and by not clinging, he would not be agitated.
mn138:22.3: When this is the case, there is no coming to be of the origin of suffering—of rebirth, old age, and death in the future.’
mn138:22.4: And this is how I understand the detailed meaning of this summary recital.
mn138:22.5: If you wish, you may go to the Buddha and ask him about this.
mn138:22.6: You should remember it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”
mn138:23.1: Then those bhikkhus, approving and agreeing with what Mahākaccāna said, rose from their seats and went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding:
mn138:23.15: “Mahākaccāna clearly explained the meaning to us in this manner, with these words and phrases.”
mn138:24.1: “Mahākaccāna is astute, bhikkhus, he has great wisdom.
mn138:24.2: If you came to me and asked this question, I would answer it in exactly the same way as Mahākaccāna.
mn138:24.3: That is what it means, and that’s how you should remember it.”
mn138:24.4: That is what the Buddha said.
mn138:24.5: Satisfied, the bhikkhus approved what the Buddha said.
